content.title: Using Dashes for Insertions and Abrupt Shifts
content.overview: Dashes (specifically em dashes) are versatile punctuation marks used to set off interrupting thoughts, provide emphasis, or signal an abrupt shift in a sentence. While they function similarly to commas or parentheses, dashes create a stronger, more dramatic break in the flow of the sentence.
learning_objectives: Identify internal interrupting phrases that require isolation.
Apply the Dash Isolate-and-Emphasize strategy to set off nonessential information.
Recognize and correct inconsistent punctuation, such as mixing a comma with a dash.
Determine when a dash is appropriate for signaling a sudden change in direction or tone.

sections.title: The Dash Isolate-and-Emphasize Strategy
sections.content: When a sentence contains an internal comment, an extra detail, or a sudden shift, you can use dashes to spotlight that information. If the interruption occurs in the middle of a sentence, it must be framed by a pair of dashes—one at the start and one at the end. This isolation tells the reader to pause briefly and pay extra attention to the enclosed content. Unlike commas, which provide a soft pause, dashes create a sharp, emphatic break.

sections.title: Punctuation Consistency and Redundancy
sections.content: A critical rule for the ACT is punctuation consistency. You should never 'mix and match' punctuation marks to set off the same phrase. If you start an interruption with a dash, you must end it with a dash. Furthermore, do not use commas and dashes together to frame the same phrase; the dash replaces the comma entirely to avoid redundancy.

sections.title: Abrupt Shifts and Emphasis
sections.content: Dashes can also be used to signal a sudden change in thought or a dramatic conclusion at the end of a sentence. In these cases, a single dash acts as a bridge between the main clause and the abrupt shift. This is often used to add a 'punchline' or a surprising clarification that deviates from the expected path of the sentence.

worked_examples.question: Choose the best revision for the underlined portion: The scientist, despite years of failure — finally discovered the cure for the rare disease.
worked_examples.solution: 1. Identify the interruption: 'despite years of failure' is an internal comment. 2. Check for consistency: The sentence currently uses a comma at the start and a dash at the end. This is inconsistent. 3. Apply the rule: Either use two commas or two dashes. Looking at the options (implied), using two dashes emphasizes the struggle. 4. Correct version: 'The scientist—despite years of failure—finally discovered the cure...'

worked_examples.question: Which version correctly uses a dash for an abrupt shift? A) The cake was delicious, but—it was gone. B) The cake was delicious—but it was gone. C) The cake was delicious—it was gone.
worked_examples.solution: 1. Analyze the shift: The speaker is moving from a positive description to a sudden realization of loss. 2. Evaluate B: The dash is placed before the conjunction 'but', which is redundant. 3. Evaluate C: The dash correctly bridges the main thought and the sudden, emphatic conclusion. Correct version: 'The cake was delicious—it was gone.'

common_mistakes: Mixing punctuation: Using a comma to open an interruption and a dash to close it (or vice versa).
Over-punctuation: Placing a comma immediately before or after a dash.
Fragmenting: Using a dash in a way that leaves the main clause without a subject or a verb.
Misplacing the dash: Putting the dash inside the interrupting phrase rather than around it.
exam_tips: If you see a dash in the non-underlined portion of a sentence, look for its 'partner' dash in the underlined portion.
Read the sentence without the phrase between the dashes; the remaining sentence must be grammatically complete.
Dashes are more 'dramatic' than commas. If the ACT asks you to choose between them and both are grammatically correct, look for context clues suggesting emphasis or a sudden break.
content.recap: Dashes are used to isolate and emphasize interruptions or abrupt shifts. When used mid-sentence, they must come in pairs. Never mix a dash with a comma to set off the same phrase, and ensure the main sentence remains functional if the dashed material is removed.

knowledge_claims.content: To isolate an internal interrupting phrase with dashes, place one dash immediately before the phrase and a matching dash immediately after it.
When using dashes to set off a phrase, all surrounding commas that would have framed that same phrase must be removed.
Dashes create a stronger, more emphatic, or more abrupt break in a sentence compared to commas or parentheses.
A sentence is grammatically sound if the text between two matching dashes can be removed and the remaining parts form a complete, logical sentence.
It is a punctuation error to use a comma to start an interruption and a dash to end it.
A single dash near the end of a sentence typically signals a sudden shift in thought or a dramatic concluding comment.
An abrupt shift is recognized as a sudden change in direction, tone, or logic within a single sentence.
Punctuation marks used to set off a parenthetical element must be identical (e.g., two dashes or two commas, not one of each).
Dashes should be used when the writer intends to spotlight or draw specific attention to the inserted information.
Do not place a dash immediately after a coordinating conjunction like 'and' or 'but' when signaling a shift.
In the context of ACT punctuation, an 'insertion' is a nonessential phrase or comment added into the middle of a clause.
If a dash appears in the non-underlined text, the corresponding underlined portion likely requires a matching dash to maintain consistency.

Practice form 1. Rina is editing a short report about a community garden.

Which choice uses dashes correctly?

options.A: One result—the sudden drop at noon required further study.
options.B: One result the sudden drop—at noon—required further study.
options.C: One result—the sudden drop at noon—required further study.
options.D: One result, the sudden drop at noon—required further study.

items.explanation: The correct choice directly applies the target skill: 破折号标示插入、强调或转折.

videoLesson.title: Isolate And Emphasize With Dashes
videoLesson.description: You will recognize interrupting phrases set off by dashes and the absence of surrounding commas. Place matching dashes around the interruption and omit commas to create an emphatic, abrupt break.
